reference.source: GeneReviews / Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Caused by a supernumerary isochromosome made up of two short arms of chromosome 18, giving four copies of 18p
Presents with developmental delay or intellectual disability, usually moderate, with frequent speech delay
Neonatal feeding difficulties and hypotonia, sometimes later evolving into spasticity, are common
Microcephaly and characteristic facial features such as a narrow or oval face, strabismus, and a high nasal bridge are typical
Behavioural difficulties and, in some, a movement disorder or seizures may occur
Growth restriction and low birth weight are frequent
The isochromosome usually arises de novo, most often from a maternal meiotic error, so recurrence risk is low but not zero
reference.pathophysiology: Tetrasomy 18p results from a supernumerary marker chromosome that is an isochromosome of the short arm of chromosome 18, so that four copies of 18p are present, comprising the two normal chromosome 18s plus the two arms of the isochromosome. The extra dosage of genes on 18p disturbs neurodevelopment and growth, producing the characteristic pattern of intellectual disability, hypotonia evolving to spasticity, and dysmorphism. It generally occurs sporadically through a meiotic or post-meiotic error, commonly of maternal origin.
additionalDifferentials: 18p deletion syndrome, which reflects the opposite dosage change
Cerebral palsy, given the tone abnormalities
additionalInvestigations: Karyotype to identify the marker chromosome
FISH or microarray to confirm the marker is derived from 18p
Chromosomal microarray to characterise copy number
MRI of the brain if seizures or a movement disorder are present
Developmental and speech and language assessment
Feeding and swallow evaluation in infancy
redFlags: Severe neonatal feeding difficulty with failure to thrive
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is generally not markedly reduced; most individuals have moderate intellectual disability with ongoing motor and speech difficulties, and outcome depends on the severity of neurological involvement.
pitfalls: Reporting a marker chromosome without identifying its origin, which requires FISH or microarray
Misattributing tone abnormalities to cerebral palsy without cytogenetic testing
Overlooking spasticity that evolves after initial hypotonia
Assuming a high recurrence risk when most cases are de novo
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Gardner and Sutherland's Chromosome Abnormalities and Genetic Counseling
